summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
Per GAO audits federal AI use, twenty of 23 major federal agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of those reported use cases were in the planning phase rather than in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported that they were currently using AI. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases.

GAO's inventory shows the uses skew toward analysis and detection. Agencies reported using AI to analyze data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, to analyze photographs from drones, and to target scientific specimens for planetary rovers. Some agencies are also using AI operationally to identify information security threats and to facilitate the review of large datasets.

On funding, GAO notes the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. The excerpts do not identify vendor concentration or procurement winners in the government sector.

GAO found that federal AI management is incomplete. There is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and the Office of Management and Budget has not yet developed that guidance. The Office of Personnel Management has not established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy did not communicate which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements. GAO also identified incomplete and inaccurate data in agency inventories, with only five agencies providing comprehensive information for each reported use case.

Per the AI laws tracker on theworldofai.org, 5,948 artificial intelligence bills are tracked across 53 jurisdictions, and a comparison of enrolled measures found 101 measures across 27 states as of September 18, 2026. No state created a new agency to enforce AI law; the attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively. The recurring duties are to tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits or education, have a crisis protocol for conversational products, and keep records. Stanford HAI's AI Index reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared governments are to manage it, with frameworks for governance, evaluation, and understanding falling behind, and notes that data transparency is declining. OECD.AI gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, and Oxford Insights ranks national readiness, but the excerpts do not provide specific scores.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy AI in government, the record shows early and mostly planned adoption, incomplete federal oversight, and a state-by-state patchwork of duties. Build to the common core that recurs across state laws, expect the attorney general as the most likely enforcer, and keep a qualified human in consequential decisions.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports tracking 5,934 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, with data refreshed daily from LegiScan and linked to each bill’s official page. It also compares 101 enacted measures across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026, and finds that no two states wrote the same law. Recurring rules include requiring human involvement in high-stakes decisions such as insurance denials, therapy, and benefit determinations, while no state in the set created a new enforcement agency. The page notes that attorneys general most often enforce the larger laws, and private rights to sue are rare, appearing mainly where one identifiable person is harmed.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
